chapter_theme: The king calls his ministers into the sealed council hall and tells them that kings rule through counsel and the learned, then asks who could match his daughter's worth; the ministers bow, and Sachchutan and others begin to answer in turn with images of gem and sun and sandal.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, who holds council
the Vidyadhara king's counsellors, summoned to the council hall
the minister who first answers the king

239.reading: The king's word reaches the learned counsellors, who tremble at it and come to his feet.
239.nuance: The words that open the verse name the king only by an epithet, and the poison-bright spear in line 4 names him again; that both are the same king, who spoke at the end of the last section, is the likely reading.
239.event: The king's summons reaches his ministers, who come in fear to the king.

240.reading: The poet describes the council hall as a closed place with a silver-rimmed platform, where no sound leaves and neither bird nor anything else comes in.
240.nuance: Line 2 names only birds and 'what are not birds' as barred; the poet gives no reason, and the closing of the hall to sound is the plain point.

241.reading: The king and his ministers go into the fragrant hall and sit, and the king, earrings flashing, begins to speak.
241.event: The king and his ministers enter the hall and sit, and the king begins to speak.

242.reading: The king says that even kings of good nature can grasp subtle meanings only through the fine treatises the learned have composed, and that none decides on his own thought.
242.nuance: The verse ranks the treatise above the king's own discernment; it does not say that books alone suffice for acting.

claims.claim: a king, however virtuous, can understand subtle matters only through the treatises of the learned and has no counsel of his own to decide by

243.reading: The king says that though he guards the whole sea-ringed earth with an unbent sceptre, it is the learned of the books who stand to keep later blame and fierce deeds away from him.

claims.claim: the learned guard even a just king from later blame and from cruel deeds

244.reading: The king says that though he sits crowned under the white umbrella, his mind, his eye, his living, his strength, his worth and his rule and sceptre belong to his ministers.
244.nuance: Line 4 gives the ministers an epithet, மாபவர், that can be read as 'of great penance' or as 'great ones'; either way the weight falls on their share in his rule.

claims.claim: a king's mind, sight, strength, rule and sceptre depend on his ministers

245.reading: The king says a single yoke cannot carry the whole watery world, but it can be borne when learned counsellors, who plan how rivals will bow, share the load with the ruler.

claims.claim: a king cannot bear the world alone and bears it with the learned beside him

246.reading: The king says that a king who has taken up the hard work of guarding the world must pass it as the learned direct, and that those who see his good, keep blame far off and break proud foes are the wise in counsel.
246.nuance: The last two lines are compressed and the link between the 'good' sought for him and the foes' pride is not spelled out.

claims.claim: a king's duty is to carry out his rule as the learned have taught
the counsellor's task is to seek the king's good, keep blame from him and break proud foes

247.reading: The king says he is a king who calmly acts on what well-read learned men choose and tell him, and that ministers are those who tell him so and then carry it out.
247.nuance: Lines 1-2 and 3-4 say nearly the same in the same words, one for the king and one for the minister; the poem sets the two offices side by side.

claims.claim: a king is one who acts calmly on what the learned advise
a minister is one who both advises and carries out what the learned choose

248.reading: The king says that kings win the world by two powers, strength of arm and counsel, and that though the armed host is fine, he tells lion-like ministers that counsel is the quality that counts.

claims.claim: counsel is a better power than strength of arm for a king who would win the world

249.reading: The king says that even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of those who take counsel, and that those who live by counsel, if skilled, flourish as kings.
249.nuance: ஊழ் வர அன்னது is condensed. The sense may be 'even an act that fate has set is shown through counsel', not that counsel overturns fate; the verse does not say a former deed is meant.

claims.claim: even what arrives like fate takes shape in deliberation, and those skilled in counsel rise as kings

250.reading: The king says that of the three powers taught for kings, counsel is the highest, so a king who sits and goes with able ministers meets nothing hard.
250.nuance: The verse does not name the three powers.

claims.claim: counsel is the highest of a king's three powers, and a king guided by able ministers finds nothing too hard

251.reading: The king says that kings maddened with love of the women who wear necklaces, if they have no learned men to join them, are like a rutting elephant flushed with pride and ridden by a fool without learning.
251.nuance: Line 4's image is hard to construe: the rider is read here as a fool who has mounted the elephant.

claims.claim: a king who gives himself to women and has no learned counsellors is out of control like a rutting elephant under an ignorant rider

252.reading: The king says that kings must lean on counsel, and that if counsel slips, it turns on the king like an angry fanged snake whose charmer's art has failed.
252.nuance: தந்திரம் in line 4 could be the charmer's art or a rule of statecraft; the snake image fits the first better.

claims.claim: a king must rely on counsel, and failed counsel destroys him

253.reading: The king says that a jewel of fair birth takes the colour of what it lies on like a crystal, and that so the good deeds of the learned are counted as the king's own virtues.
253.nuance: Lines 1-3 are knotted; the verse is read here as a crystal taking its hue from what lies beside it, not as a claim that the ministers are flawless.

claims.claim: a king is credited with the virtues shown in his ministers' work

254.reading: The king tells the ministers it is useless to say more, since they made him king by their daily work, and that through them he has risen into a flood of joy.
254.event: The king thanks the ministers and says he owes his kingship and his joy to their work.

255.reading: The king asks who could match the worth of the maiden born to light his house like a lamp on a diamond hill, and in what way he must stand so that his own house shines.
255.nuance: The verse names no marriage; the question of who is her match is read here from the lamp image and the word நங்கை, 'the woman', and the poem's turn to a Vidyadhara match elsewhere in the section.
255.event: The king puts to the ministers the question of the fit husband for the maiden who lights their house.

256.reading: The ministers hear the king, bow and praise him, wish him a long, widely praised rule over the earth, and each in turn prepares to speak.
256.event: The ministers bow, praise the king and prepare to speak in turn.

257.reading: One minister, Sachchutan, bows while the others sit aside, studies the many treatises, and begins to speak with humility before the king in his gem crown and green garland.
257.nuance: Line 2 says he speaks out of 'his own lowliness'; the humility is a convention of address.
257.event: The minister Sachchutan bows to the king and begins to speak.

258.reading: Sachchutan tells the king that the sun-gem spits fire when the sun appears and scatters the night's dark, and addresses him as the king of kings with the blazing spear.
258.nuance: The verse gives only the image; the application to the king and his ministers is drawn in verse 259.

259.reading: Sachchutan says that by the grace of kings who guard the order of command and treatise, the worth of the learned poets grows, as the sacred thread shows bright on the chest of the golden-chested king.
259.nuance: Lines 1-2 are dense; the sense taken is that kings who keep the rule of treatise draw out the worth of those who follow it, as the sun draws fire from the sun-gem in 258.

claims.claim: the standing of the learned grows through the grace of kings who guard the law of command and treatise

260.reading: A minister tells the king that the moon-gem pours a flood of water when the moon god rises and sheds cool rays, and addresses him as the spear-bearer who pours out flesh and fat.
260.nuance: Line 4 turns from the cool image to the spear that sheds the flesh and fat of foes. The speaker is the next minister in the turn announced in 256, and is not named.

261.reading: The minister says that by the merit of kings who guard the world with a gracious straight sceptre, the counsel of learned men blossoms, and he speaks it to the king under the white umbrella.
261.nuance: தவம் here may mean the austerity or merit of the king, not a former deed; the verse does not say.

claims.claim: the counsel of the learned flowers through the merit of kings who rule with a straight sceptre

262.reading: The speaker says that as sandal keeps its coolness though a rutting elephant rubs against it, so if the virtuous masters bear the lapses of the lowly, the whole earth follows and bows to them.
262.nuance: This verse has no closing என்றான் and may belong to a third minister's speech; the speaker is read here as the same unnamed minister as 260-261.

claims.claim: lords who bear the lapses of the lowly are followed and honoured by the whole earth

links.note: Verse 242 has the king say he can grasp subtle things only through the learned treatises; Kural 637 says that even one who knows the method must act by knowing how the world goes.
links.teaches: The council's first claim makes the treatise the king's only guide, where the couplet warns that a treatise's method must still be tested against the world, so the two disagree on where good judgment is found.

gains.a: A corrective: the books the king defers to still leave him to read the world's own way.
gains.b: A case for deference: why a ruler should hold a treatise above his own sense.

links.note: Verse 243 says the learned keep blame and fierce deeds from a king whose sceptre is unbent; Kural 547 says justice guards the king if he does not falter in it.
links.teaches: The epic names who keeps a king from faltering, the learned counsellors, where the couplet names only the law that guards him if he does not.

gains.a: A reason why the sceptre stays unbent: it is kept by the learned.
gains.b: Persons who do the guarding the couplet gives to justice itself.

links.note: Verse 244 makes the ministers the king's mind, eye, living, strength and sceptre; Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes and says he must take them after testing them.
links.teaches: The epic widens the Kural's single image of eyes to the king's whole body of rule, while the couplet adds a duty of choosing that the epic leaves unsaid.

gains.a: A rule for choosing: the king must test his counsellors before taking them.
gains.b: A fuller count of what rests on counsellors, from sight to the sceptre itself.

links.note: Verse 247 makes a king one who acts calmly on what the learned choose and tell him; Kural 638 says the man at the king's side must tell him what is good even if the king knows nothing and spoils wise counsel.
links.teaches: The epic sets the king's duty to act on counsel beside the minister's duty to give it, where the couplet shows only the minister's duty when the king will not hear.

gains.a: A case where the king refuses counsel and the minister must still speak.
gains.b: A test of kingship: the king's standing comes from acting calmly on the counsel he is given.

links.note: Verse 248 says counsel, not strength of arm, is the quality of a king; Kural 546 says it is not the spear but the unbent sceptre that gives victory.
links.teaches: Each puts a different power above the weapon, counsel in the epic and justice in the couplet, so the pair shows that the Tamil tradition names more than one winner of a war.

gains.a: A moral check: counsel that is clever but crooked would still fail the sceptre's test.
gains.b: A practical account of how victory is planned, where the couplet gives only its moral condition.

links.note: Verse 249 says even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of counsellors; Kural 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back.
links.teaches: The epic puts fate and effort together in the council hall and finds that deliberation is where fate takes shape, while the couplet says effort can turn fate back.

gains.a: A place where fate and effort meet: counsel, not only labour, is the effort.
gains.b: A limit on its boast: effort works through counsel, and counsel is the stage on which fate shows.

links.note: Verse 249 says what comes like fate takes shape in the counsellors' deliberation; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
links.teaches: The epic lets fate arrive through chosen acts of counsel, while the quatrain says the old deed finds its doer whatever he does, so the two differ on how far deliberation shapes what comes.

gains.a: The unavoidable pursuit by an old deed, which the verse softens by placing fate in counsel.
gains.b: A route by which an old deed arrives: through the choices of counsellors.

links.note: Verse 237 says that without counsel a king's life does not flourish and that even Indra's lordship rests on a thousand counsellors; verse 250 has the king himself rank counsel above his other powers.
links.teaches: The poet's maxim about counsel becomes the king's own weighing of counsel against his other powers, so the section turns a reflection into a decision.

links.note: Verse 251 compares a king in love's grip without learned men to a rutting elephant ridden by a fool; Cintamani 9 tells of a king whose dense desire made him refuse counsel and lose to a plot.
links.teaches: The Cintamani's story gives the cost that the Soolamani's maxim only warns of, a king who would not hear and lost the throne.

links.note: Verse 252 says failed counsel turns on the king like an angry snake whose charmer's art has failed; Kural 448 says a king with none to rebuke him perishes even without a foe.
links.teaches: The epic shows a king with counsellors destroyed by counsel gone wrong, where the couplet shows a king destroyed by having no counsellor who dares to rebuke him.

gains.a: A king who had counsellors and still fell: counsel itself can fail.
gains.b: A picture of how the king ruins himself: the instrument turns on the user.

links.note: Verse 254 has the king thank the ministers for his rule; Cintamani 206 has a counsellor press the king to hear counsel he does not want.
links.teaches: The Soolamani's council shows a king who welcomes counsel, while the Cintamani shows the counsellor who must speak when the king would not listen, so the ideal depends on a willing king.

links.note: Verse 140 names the one fault of the Vidyadhara king as want of grace toward the lowly; verse 262 has a minister say that great lords who bear the lapses of the lowly are followed by the whole earth.
links.teaches: The council offers the remedy for the king's single fault, so the earlier flaw reads as a fault the poem expects the counsellors to mend.

links.note: Verse 262 says lords who bear the lowly's lapses, like sandal under the rutting elephant, are bowed to by the earth; Naladiyar 66 says the well-born bear the base's stone-like words and let them pass, held back by their lineage.
links.teaches: The epic names the reward of forbearance in the king's public standing, where the quatrain names its reason in birth.

gains.a: The reward of forbearance in public honour, which the image alone does not name.
gains.b: A political result for the restraint that the quatrain justifies only by lineage.

source_issues: Verses 239-240, 244, 246, 249, 251-253, 255, 259-260, 262: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain.
Verse 262 has no closing என்றான் and its speaker is not stated; verse 255 does not name the marriage.
